summary: A major power in East Asia, namely the People's Republic of China, with a civilization of several thousand years; its population is second only to India's, and after the reform and opening-up of 1978 it became the world's second-largest economy.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Chinese history was dominated by Confucian ethics and ancestor worship, and unlike Europe there was no single exclusive religious organization. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the Chinese Communist Party took Marxist atheism as its official ideology; during the Cultural Revolution of 1966–1976 temples and churches were destroyed on a large scale and religious activity almost entirely stopped. Although limited religious freedom was restored after the reform and opening-up, Party members may not hold religious beliefs and schools promote atheist education, so about half the population identify as non-religious.

ranking.name: Folk religion
ranking.description: Folk religion includes ancestor worship, belief in local deities such as the Earth God (Tudigong), Mazu, Guan Gong and the God of Wealth, and customs such as feng shui and fortune-telling; it originates in the ancestral-spirit and nature worship of high antiquity and has blended with Taoism and Buddhism. During the Cultural Revolution folk religion was regarded as 'feudal superstition' and destroyed, but from the 1980s it revived greatly in places such as Fujian, Guangdong and Zhejiang on the southeast coast, and many people sweep tombs at the Qingming Festival and make ancestral offerings at the Spring Festival.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism was introduced to China from India via Central Asia in the Eastern Han period (traditionally in AD 67, when the White Horse Temple was built under Emperor Ming of Han), reached its peak in the Wei, Jin, Northern and Southern Dynasties and the Sui and Tang periods, and formed Sinicized schools such as Chan (Zen) and Pure Land. The 'Huichang persecution of Buddhism' by Emperor Wuzong of Tang in 845 and political blows in successive dynasties caused Buddhism to decline at times, but it blended with Confucianism and Taoism to become part of Chinese culture; Tibetan Buddhism is the main religion in regions such as Tibet, Qinghai and Inner Mongolia.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity arrived in the Tang dynasty in the form of Nestorianism (the Nestorian Stele was erected in 781), the Jesuit Matteo Ricci came to China to preach in the late 16th century, and after the Opium War in the 19th century the unequal treaties allowed missionaries to preach across China. After 1949 foreign missionaries were expelled and the government set up the Three-Self Patriotic Movement to manage Protestantism, but after the reform and opening-up unregistered 'house churches' grew rapidly, especially in provinces such as Henan and Zhejiang.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced in the Tang dynasty by Arab and Persian merchants along the maritime and overland Silk Roads, and the Huaisheng Mosque in Guangzhou is said to have been built in the Tang. In the Yuan dynasty large numbers of Central Asian Muslims moved in and gradually formed the Hui people. Today Muslims mainly include the Hui and the Uyghurs and Kazakhs of Xinjiang, concentrated in Xinjiang, Ningxia, Gansu and Qinghai. Since 2017 the government has implemented policies of mass detention and religious restriction in Xinjiang, which have been widely criticized by the international community.

religion.background: Since the Shang and Zhou periods China has had sacrifices to Heaven and ancestor worship; in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods Confucian and Taoist thought arose, and in the Eastern Han Buddhism was introduced and religious Taoism formed, and over the following two thousand years the three blended into the tradition of the 'unity of the three teachings'. From the Tang dynasty Islam and Nestorianism arrived, in the Ming and Qing periods Catholicism came with the Jesuits, and in the 19th century Protestantism spread with the expansion of Western powers. After the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 the state took atheism as its ideology and suppressed religion across the board during the Cultural Revolution. After the reform and opening-up of 1978 religion recovered somewhat, but remains under strict state management, and the government recognizes only five major religions: Buddhism, Taoism, Islam, Catholicism and Protestantism.

language.official: The official language is Modern Standard Chinese (Putonghua, Mandarin).

ranking.name: Mandarin (including northern dialects)
ranking.description: Mandarin is a group of dialects based on northern Chinese, spoken north of the Yangtze and in the southwestern provinces. Under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties Beijing was the capital, and the Beijing dialect became the officials' common language, 'guanhua'. In 1913 the Conference on the Unification of Pronunciation of the Republic began to promote a national language, and in 1955 the People's Republic of China, taking Beijing pronunciation as the standard sound and northern dialects as the base dialect, established 'Putonghua' and promoted it vigorously through education and the media, so that the population using northern Mandarin accounts for about 70%.

ranking.name: Wu
ranking.description: Wu is the dialect of Shanghai, Suzhou, Hangzhou and Zhejiang, and preserves many of the voiced-consonant features of Middle Chinese. The lower Yangtze delta has been China's wealthiest region since the Song dynasty, and Wu was also the language of Kunqu opera and Suzhou pingtan storytelling. But with the promotion of Putonghua, the younger generation in cities such as Shanghai speaks Wu less and less.

ranking.name: Cantonese
ranking.description: Cantonese is spoken in Guangdong, parts of Guangxi, Hong Kong and Macao, and preserves the entering tones of Middle Chinese and its nine tones in six tone categories. After migrants from the Central Plains entered Lingnan in the Qin and Han periods and merged with the local Baiyue peoples, Cantonese gradually formed. Hong Kong's films and popular music in the latter half of the 20th century made Cantonese widely popular among overseas Chinese, and overseas migration after the 19th century also carried Cantonese to Southeast Asia and North America.

ranking.name: Min
ranking.description: Min includes Southern Min (Hokkien), Eastern Min (the Fuzhou dialect) and others, mainly spoken in Fujian, the Chaoshan area of Guangdong, and Hainan; Southern Min also spread to Taiwan and Southeast Asia through migration in the Ming and Qing periods. Min is thought to preserve the most features of Old and Middle Chinese and is the most divergent branch among the Chinese dialects.

ranking.name: Hakka
ranking.description: Hakka is the language of the Hakka people, whose ancestors are said to be Han Chinese who moved gradually south from the Central Plains after the 'Yongjia disturbance' at the end of the Western Jin and in the wars at the end of the Tang and the Song. The Hakka live mainly in the mountain areas of northeastern Guangdong, western Fujian and southern Jiangxi, and after the Qing dynasty large numbers moved to Taiwan, Southeast Asia and elsewhere.

language.history: Chinese has more than three thousand years of written records, and the oracle-bone script of the Shang dynasty is the earliest known mature Chinese writing. The First Emperor of Qin unified the script in 221 BC, after which Chinese characters became a writing system that crosses dialects, while the spoken languages of various regions continued to diverge into dialects such as Mandarin, Wu, Cantonese, Min and Hakka. The vernacular-language movement of the early 20th century (from 1917) moved the written language from Classical Chinese to vernacular Chinese. In the 1950s the People's Republic of China introduced simplified characters, Hanyu Pinyin and Putonghua, making Putonghua the nationwide common language, but this also reduced the number of speakers of some dialects. China also has minority languages such as Tibetan, Uyghur and Mongolian.

ranking.name: Peking duck
ranking.description: A force-fed duck is roasted in a hanging oven or closed oven until the skin is crisp and glossy red, sliced thin, and rolled in thin pancakes with sweet bean sauce and scallion strips.
ranking.history: Roast duck is recorded in the Southern Song period at Lin'an (present-day Hangzhou), and after the Ming court moved the capital to Beijing (1421), the court brought the roast-duck technique of Nanjing to Beijing. Bianyifang, founded in 1416, is known for closed-oven roast duck, while Quanjude, founded in 1864, is famous for hanging-oven roast duck. After 1949 Peking duck became a state banquet dish, and when US President Nixon visited China in 1972 it was served to him, since which it has become one of China's international signature dishes.

ranking.name: Jiaozi (dumplings)
ranking.description: Thin wrappers rolled from flour are filled with pork, napa cabbage, chives and other fillings, pinched into half-moons and boiled, steamed or pan-fried, often dipped in vinegar and mashed garlic.
ranking.history: Jiaozi are said to have been invented by the famous Eastern Han physician Zhang Zhongjing to treat frostbitten ears, and so were called 'jiao'er' (tender ears); well-preserved dumplings have also been unearthed from a Tang-dynasty tomb in Turpan, Xinjiang. Because the shape of jiaozi resembles ancient ingot money, northerners eat jiaozi on New Year's Eve, symbolizing 'the turn of the year' and bringing wealth, and making jiaozi has become an important family reunion activity.

ranking.name: Mapo tofu
ranking.description: Tofu is braised with ground beef or pork in doubanjiang (chili bean paste), chili and Sichuan pepper, with a flavor that is numbing, spicy, hot, fragrant, crisp and tender, a representative Sichuan dish.
ranking.history: Mapo tofu is said to originate in the Tongzhi era of the Qing dynasty (1860s) in a small restaurant at Wanfu Bridge in the northern suburbs of Chengdu; the proprietress, Chen Liu-shi, had pockmarks on her face and was known as 'Pockmarked Chen' (Chen Mapo), and the tofu she cooked for oil carriers and coolies was a great success, hence the name. Sichuan pepper is a traditional local spice of Sichuan, while chili peppers were brought to China by sea from the Americas in the late Ming and only became widespread in Sichuan after the Qing. The dish later spread with Sichuan cuisine across China and the world.

ranking.name: Xiaolongbao (soup dumplings)
ranking.description: A thin wheat wrapper is filled with pork filling and aspic made from pork skin; once steamed the aspic melts into broth inside the wrapper, so that a bite floods the mouth with soup, often dipped in vinegar with shredded ginger.
ranking.history: Xiaolongbao originated in the Jiangnan region in the Qing dynasty and is generally thought to have been created by Huang Mingxian of Nanxiang Town in Jiading, Shanghai, in the Tongzhi era (1870s), called 'Nanxiang xiaolong'. Adding aspic made from pork skin, which produces broth when steamed, is the technical key. With Shanghai and Jiangnan migrants in the 20th century, xiaolongbao spread to Taiwan, Hong Kong and elsewhere, and Taiwan's Din Tai Fung made it famous internationally.

ranking.name: Kung Pao chicken
ranking.description: Diced chicken is quick-fried with peanuts, dried chilies and Sichuan pepper, with a sweet, sour and mildly spicy sauce made from soy sauce, vinegar and sugar, salty, savory and spicy.
ranking.history: Kung Pao chicken is named after Ding Baozhen, the Qing-dynasty governor-general of Sichuan, whose official title 'Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince' was honorifically called 'Gongbao'. It is said that Ding Baozhen loved this dish while serving in Guizhou and Shandong and later promoted it in Sichuan, making it a famous Sichuan dish. During the Cultural Revolution, because 'Gongbao' carried the flavor of a feudal official title, it was for a time renamed 'Hula chicken cubes'. After the 19th century it spread overseas with Chinese emigrants and became 'Kung Pao Chicken' in American Chinese cuisine.
